title: Predictable throughput SLA negotiation guide
body:
Purpose:
This is a practical negotiation and messaging guide for sales, AE engineering, and solutions teams when discussing Redwood Dedicated capacity commitments. Focus: predictable throughput, hard isolation, SLA commitments that procurement/legal can sign, and an operational path for onboarding and exit.

Audience and primary buyer personas:
- Platform Architect / Infrastructure Lead (Mid-market / Enterprise) — cares about isolation, predictable tail latency, and predictable unit economics.
- ML/Inference Ops (ML infra, CTO-level for startups) — cares about model compatibility, runtime observability, and KV-cache behavior under burst.
- Procurement / Legal — wants clear SLO language, remedies, and termination triggers.
- Cloud/Platform PMs (evaluation stage) — will compare against reserved cloud GPU contracts and self-hosting.

One-line sales opener (elevator pitch):
"Redwood Dedicated gives you production-grade inference with contract-level throughput guarantees, tenant-grade isolation, and a clear procurement path so your team can ship latency-sensitive LLM features without running the whole stack."

Core promises to land in conversation (short bullets for reps):
- Predictable throughput: committed throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec) backed by measurable capacity allocation and a ramp plan.
- Isolation: dedicated GPU pools, isolated KV cache and storage, tenant-level networking controls (VPC), no noisy-neighbor interference.
- Latency SLOs: percentile-based latency commitments (examples below) with reporting and credits for breaches.
- Procurement-ready terms: clear definitions for measurement, remedies, maintenance windows, and exit/portability.

SLA and SLO examples (worded to be procurement-friendly):
- Availability SLO: 99.95% monthly availability for Dedicated control/serving plane (customer-facing endpoint). Remedy: service credits tiered by severity (5–20% of monthly commitment).
- Tail latency SLO: 95th percentile response latency <= 200ms for <512 token requests under committed throughput; 99th percentile <= 700ms. Remedy: incremental credits + joint remediation plan.
- Throughput guarantee: committed baseline of N tokens/sec (or M requests/sec) sustained for business hours (customer-defined window) with burst bucket for occasional spikes up to 2x baseline for short windows. Remedy: pro-rated credits for sustained shortfalls and immediate scale-to-fallback routing to a compatible variant.
- Isolation guarantee: dedicated physical/virtual GPU assignment and network isolation for all committed capacity; proof via audit logs and tenant topology diagrams during onboarding.

Operational artifacts to attach to procurement package (include as appendices):
- Capacity allocation diagram (how many GPU units, instance types, peak token/sec expectations).
- Ramp schedule and capacity acceptance test (CAT) checklist (30/60/90-day ramp milestones).
- Maintenance window policy and planned outage calendar (quarterly maintenance limits).
- Incident escalation matrix and RCA cadence.
- Data handling and encryption commitments (KMS/HSM integration notes).
- Exit plan: model state export, KV cache wipe, recommended migration checklist.

Negotiation playbook (step-by-step):
1) Anchor on reliability: start with availability + tail latency numbers rather than raw GPU counts. Procurement cares about business impact more than instance SKU.
2) Offer a 3-tier commitment model: Pilot (time-limited, lower commit, faster onboarding), Standard (12-month commit, base SLA), Enterprise (annual commit, higher SLA, prioritized SRE).
3) For price discussions, use throughput as the unit: $/committed-token/sec or $/reserved-GPU-equivalent. Always map back to customer workload (tokens per user, peak concurrency).
4) Define clear acceptance tests: run customer-defined queries under target load in a staging window and capture telemetry. Sign-off moves to billing when acceptance passed.
5) Provide a burst policy and an overage pricing cap to reduce resistance — limited bursts billed at a predictable premium rather than opaque cloud egress style fees.
6) Negotiate remedies, not absolute uptime: service credits + joint remediation + escalation path. Keep financial penalties proportional.

Competitive positioning notes (how to differentiate succinctly):
- Vs hyperscaler managed endpoints: Hyperscalers sell VMs — but often no contract-level per-tenant throughput guarantee for inference workloads; Redwood pairs a high-throughput inference runtime with legalized SLOs and faster model-specific optimizations (quantization/kv-cache).
- Vs LLM-API incumbents: Many API providers offer single-tenant options but lack prescriptive procurement artifacts (ramp plans, acceptance tests). Redwood bundles operational handoff, observability, and a clearly scoped exit.
- Vs self-hosting (open-source + infra): Self-hosting gives control but requires hiring SRE/infra specialization and months of tuning. Redwood abstracts that operational burden while providing the same controls and auditability with faster time-to-value.

Common procurement objections and rebuttals (quick scripts):
- "We can use reserved cloud GPUs instead." → "Reserved GPUs are a commodity; the hard part is the inference runtime, KV/cache, and SLOs across peak patterns. We guarantee throughput for your model mix and manage the runtime optimizations on day one."
- "How do we trust your measurements?" → "We provide telemetry exports, a joint acceptance test, and cryptographic audit logs for capacity allocation and control-plane actions."
- "What happens if we grow faster?" → "We include sprinted ramp milestones and a transparent burst policy with billing caps; we can convert burst to committed capacity as usage stabilizes."

Procurement clause sketches (language for legal to iterate on):
- Measurement: define measurement window, how latency is computed (end-to-end with telemetry tags), and what constitutes a breach.
- Remedies: tiered service credits applied against monthly committed fees; a remediation SLA for engineering response.
- Maintenance: maximum monthly maintenance downtime, notification lead times, and allowed emergency window.
- Data & isolation: statement that committed capacity will be logically/physically isolated from other customers; obligations for encryption and export at termination.
- Termination for cause and convenience: notice periods, data handoff timelines, and final settlement of unused committed credits.

Eng/SRE checklist for customer calls (tech to prep):
- Top models and sequence length distribution (P95 sequence length).
- Request concurrency distribution and expected peak queries per second.
- Existing authentication, VPC/KMS constraints, and logging/retention needs.
- Expected ramp (hits in 30/60/90 days) and any planned large events that require sustained bursts.
- Failure modes mapping: what to do if a model requires more KV memory than promised.

Pricing and packaging guidance for AE (battle-tested levers):
- Anchor on committed tokens/sec and map to $/k tokens/sec.
- Offer convertibility: commit length (12, 24, 36 months) with incremental discounts for longer terms and multi-region add-ons.
- Upsell levers: latency SLO uplift (higher percentile SLOs), longer retention for observability, increased burst headroom.

Sales enablement artifacts to produce (priority):
- One-pager: Procurement-ready SLA summary (1 page, legal friendly) — attach in every proposal.
- Slide set: 6-slide technical runbook + 2-slide business terms + 1-slide competitive positioning.
- Acceptance test template and sample telemetry export.
- Email playbook for procurement: intro, attachment list, suggested legal redlines.

Quick win checklist (what to ship to buyer this week):
- 1-page SLA summary (tailored to buyer, with their ramp numbers filled in).
- CAT (capacity acceptance test) template filled with their target queries.
- Draft term sheet with anchor pricing and burst policy.

Open questions & risks to validate before proposal:
- Are there network egress constraints (e.g., on-prem or regional isolation) that would change the cost model?
- Does customer require encrypted KV at rest with specific HSM integration?
- Do they expect on-call access to our SREs or prefer escalation through CSM?
- Any procurement-required certifications we don’t currently have in the requested region?

Appendix: sample metrics to include in SLO reporting exports:
- Monthly availability %, Monthly SLA credits consumed, P50/P95/P99 latency by token bucket, Sustained throughput vs committed baseline (tokens/sec time-series), Burst usage minutes and peak multiplier, Incident MTTR and RCA status.

Notes for the AE: prioritize clarity and speed. Procurement teams are process-driven — give them the structured artifacts they asked for (SLA summary, acceptance tests, exit plan). Legal will iterate; aim to keep remedies proportional and operationally actionable.

Next steps (owner: Aisha):
- Convert this doc into a 1-page SLA summary template and a negotiating checklist for AEs (due: next week).
- Sync with Legal to finalize recommended clause language for measurement and remedies (due: +2 weeks).
- Pilot the package with two near-term deals and capture feedback for a standard contract addendum (target: Q2 pilot).

Revision history: draft collab; content pulled from recent wins + SRE input.
